description: A horizontally scalable, Jellyfin-compatible video server in Go. Every task below comes from PRODUCT.md (features and roadmap), the project plan, compat/coverage-12.4.tsv and the agreed work queue. PRODUCT.md stays the source of truth for status; update this file when a slice merges.

conventions.status: done | in_progress | todo | dropped; passes is true only when done
conventions.priority: 1 is next; done tasks have none
conventions.delivery: each task goes through the build workflow (.claude/workflows/build.js): checks written first and locked, one implementer until they pass, QA and one blind adversarial review with evidence-gated findings, one fix round; then PR, CI, merge, redeploy the dogfood
conventions.differential: a task that adds or changes a route jellyfin-web or another client calls adds its requests to test/differential/requests.yaml, and any difference it keeps to compat/differences.yaml with a reason

userStories.title: Follow any playback end to end, and see why the cluster needed more workers
userStories.description: An operator must be able to see exactly where a playback stalled and why the cluster needed more workers, not only that a film is transcoding. Metrics (JS-019) give totals: stalls happened, the queue is deep. This adds one OpenTelemetry trace per playback (PlaySessionId) across the api, stream and worker processes: PlaybackInfo and its decision with reasons; each segment request and where its time went (served from the store, waited on a job, started a job); the job queued, claimed (queue time, which worker) and its ffmpeg runs with their speed; helpers started, and helpers wanted but not started for lack of a free slot; and a failover (lock lost, reap, replacement). The reasons for more workers become metrics too, which autoscaling (JS-057) scales on, so the reason it scaled is visible. Viewers keep seeing in their app that a film is transcoding and why (JS-067).
acceptanceCriteria: One trace per playback session spans the api, stream and worker processes, its context carried in the transcode job row across the Postgres handoff

Given a stalled segment (over 5 s), its trace shows which part took the time: waiting for a free slot, an encode slower than real time, the upload, or reading the store; the stall metric links to the trace (exemplar)
A failover shows the dead worker's span end and the replacement's begin in one trace
Helper decisions are traced and counted: helpers started with the job's speed, and helpers wanted but not started because no slot was free

Demand for workers is a metric with its reason (jobs waiting for a slot and how long, helpers wanted but refused, jobs below real time), and the autoscaler's input is one of these, so why the cluster grew can be read back
Log lines carry the trace id (JS-022), so a trace leads to its logs
jellyfin-web's playback info still shows transcoding, its reasons and speed (JS-067), and stays right while helpers run (the viewer's own job may have ended)
Exported over OTLP to any backend, off by default; the dogfood runs a backend and the docs show reading a stall from it
Checked with real processes: a test collector receives a playback's trace from three processes, with a stall and a failover in it
userStories.notes: Needs a design review; the homelab has no tracing backend yet (Tempo suggested). Product owner (2026-11-08): wants to trace everything through the pipeline, see where something stalled and why more workers were needed; placed before P6 (Kubernetes). JS-024 review (UX): Sessions can show the viewer's job as done while helpers encode, and no log line says a helper started.

userStories.title: User management
userStories.description: Create, delete, disable users; change passwords; preferences and configuration.
acceptanceCriteria: POST /Users/New, DELETE /Users/{id}, /Users/{id}/Policy, /Password as Jellyfin 12.4
jellyfin-web's admin user pages work
Login attempts are throttled per user and per client address, and the Policy's lockout fields work as Jellyfin 12.4's do

'admin' joins Route.Access: POST /Users/New, DELETE /Users/{userId}, POST /Users/{userId}/Policy and GET /Auth/Providers declare it; a viewer gets 403 on each and TestAccess asks (named mutant: the guard treating admin as viewer)
GET /Users answers a viewer a list of one, themselves, and an administrator everyone; POST /Users and the password routes are admin-any

Policy says only what is enforced: IsAdministrator, IsDisabled, EnableContentDownloading and the two lockout fields are stored and act; a POST changing any other field from the value GET answers is 400 naming the field and stores nothing; GET's own Policy posted back answers 204

Disabled or deleted, at once: sign-in answers the same 401, in the same time, as a wrong password; forced with real processes, every token of the user answers 401 on the next request through another api process and through stream

The last administrator: forced, two administrators each demote the other through two api processes with both statements held on the users rows until pg_stat_activity shows both waiting, then released: exactly one answers 204, the other 403, and one enabled administrator remains; the same for disable and delete (named mutant: counting administrators before the update, outside its transaction)
Passwords: changing your own needs the current one; an administrator resets another's without it; either revokes the user's other tokens, shown on a second process

A revoked device or disabled user's running stream stops: forced, a direct play of the whole file read slowly when the device is revoked or the user disabled closes within 15 seconds having sent less than the file
LoginAttemptsBeforeLockout stays -1 and a set value is not honoured, as compat/differences.yaml says (D-020); a new or changed password is refused if it is among the commonly guessed ones
userStories.notes: /Configuration moved to JS-116 (2026-11-15). Access criteria from the access model (2026-11-16). Refine with care: a throttle per client address needs a trusted-proxy setting first (behind an ingress every request has its address), and a lockout by user name lets anyone lock a known account out. State what start-up does when the configured administrator was deleted or demoted through the API.

userStories.title: Use every GPU and CPU the cluster has
userStories.description: A worker uses whatever encoder hardware its node exposes (NVIDIA NVENC, Intel QSV or VAAPI, AMD VAAPI) and falls back to the CPU, so a cluster with GPUs uses them, as Jellyfin does on the dogfood's Intel iGPUs. fMP4 can't splice across encoder families (spikes/seam: x264 spliced with NVENC lost half the frames), so each stream is given the best family with room when it starts, and its helpers (JS-024) and failover stay in that family. A GPU can also serve a CPU-encoded stream by decoding for it, if its frames equal software decoding, so every node still helps every stream.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a family is chosen for a stream, helpers and failover within a family, and what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (playing on is the goal; a restart needs the product owner's decision); and whether a copy and a re-encode should share one slot pool (today a near-free copy holds a slot for the whole film like a multi-core re-encode); and whether a GPU family re-encodes above 1080 lines, from JS-148's figures (D-021)
A worker detects at start which encoders its node can run (a short test encode per family, not the ffmpeg build's list) and advertises them; a node with no GPU runs exactly as before
A new stream gets a GPU family when a worker of that family has a free slot, and the CPU otherwise; the encoder family stays in the spec hash and the decision is logged and metered with its reason
Helpers and failover of a GPU stream stay in its family; a seek, a restart and a helper's chunk splice cleanly on QSV/VAAPI and NVENC as the seam spike showed for one family
Hardware decoding for CPU-encoded streams only where its frames are measured equal to software decoding (per codec and family); otherwise software decoding

Tested on real hardware in its own tier chosen explicitly (never skipped): Intel QSV/VAAPI on the dogfood cluster's iGPUs and NVENC on a developer machine; jellyfin-web plays, seeks and recovers from a killed GPU worker
Operators see which encoder family and worker serve each stream (Sessions, metrics, JS-021 traces)
An optional GPU worker pool requests gpu.intel.com/i915 or nvidia.com/gpu through the vendor's device plugin ; a cluster without one runs CPU workers only; documented in docs/running.md
userStories.source: PRODUCT.md phase5-library; rewritten 2026-11-08: the product owner wants every GPU and CPU in the cluster used where possible, priority kept in P5
userStories.notes: The dogfood cluster has an Intel iGPU on each of its three nodes (gpu.intel.com/i915: 1 allocatable) and the user's Jellyfin requests one; the developer machine has an RTX 4070 Ti and an AMD iGPU. GPU tone mapping (libplacebo or vendor filters) gives frames unlike zscale's, so it splices only within its own family.

userStories.title: Kubernetes example manifests
userStories.description: Example manifests an operator applies with kubectl: deployments per role, readiness and liveness, Postgres (CNPG), configuration as plain files. Split from the Helm chart (JS-142) by the direction review, 2026-11-19: an operator cannot install jellyscale today.
acceptanceCriteria: Example manifests in the repository install jellyscale on a fresh cluster with kubectl alone (`kubectl apply -k` or `-f`), no Helm
Readiness and liveness probes per role

The manifests size CNPG's max_connections from their own configuration: every process's databaseMaxConns plus the direct connections each worker holds (liveness, lease keeper, and one per running scan, segment sweep or asset sweep pass), with headroom; configuration whose sum exceeds it is refused by a check
Each probe states what it depends on: liveness never depends on Postgres or a store, so a database failover restarts no pod; ffmpeg threads follow the pod's CPU limit, not the node's cores
The worker's liveness URL can come from the environment or a Secret, and the manifests never put a password in a process's arguments
docs/running.md says which Postgres connection modes are supported (session; a transaction-mode pooler or pgx exec mode, supported or not, by a check), and the manifests connect that way
A replica whose database stays broken leaves service, and the manifests' grace period and readiness lead match the documented ones
The example manifests declare trustedProxies for their ingress (D-020)

The procedure in docs/running.md for confirming declared proxies, followed against the example manifests' ingress, says what the operator sees and does when no address is counted (every answer 401, no refusal line), and no sentence there denies a log line the server writes (D-025, BL-221)
userStories.notes: JS-020 (2026-11-08): each worker holds one Postgres connection for its liveness lock, outside the pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is exhausted at about 90 workers, long before its CPU (one primary carried 1600 streams on two cores' worth). Connections are the first wall when autoscaling. User (2026-11-08): plain manifests for kubectl are wanted beside the chart, not Helm only.

userStories.title: KEDA autoscaling
userStories.description: Scale workers on a Postgres query, keeping spare transcode slots.
acceptanceCriteria: Workers scale up under queued jobs and down when idle
KEDA's maximum worker replicas stay within the Postgres connection budget (one liveness connection per worker, on top of the pools), so scaling up never exhausts max_connections
It scales on the demand metric of JS-021 (jobs waiting for a slot, helpers refused for lack of one), so each scale-up can be read back with its reason
userStories.notes: JS-020 (2026-11-08): each worker holds one Postgres connection for its liveness lock, outside the pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is exhausted at about 90 workers, long before its CPU (one primary carried 1600 streams on two cores' worth). userStories.title: Real players on the dogfood: ExoPlayer and AVPlayer play jellyscale's own streams
userStories.description: Every streaming decision so far was checked on hls.js in Chromium only. No ExoPlayer client (Android TV, Findroid) or AVPlayer client (Swiftfin) has played a jellyscale stream, which the Phase 0 report left open (spikes/README.md, remaining risks 1 and 2), and the decision engine answers direct play to any client whose profile has no fMP4 HLS entry (internal/playback/decide.go). Before more is built on the segment format (JS-054), the owner plays films on real devices against the dogfood, and the lead records what each client asked for and what it played. Web-first stays the plan; this is a check that the format holds.
acceptanceCriteria: The owner plays, on an ExoPlayer client and on an AVPlayer client against the dogfood: a direct play, an HEVC or 4K film that transcodes, a seek, an audio switch, a text and an image subtitle

Fluster, and one client of each player family that sends its token on media requests (ExoPlayer, AVPlayer), play the same paths; an app whose player sends no token is recorded as refused by D-005, not as a failure to chase; a player family with no client that sends a token is listed in docs/status.md as not proven (no client that sends a token), a gap under D-005, not a pass
Each client's PlaybackInfo request and the server's decision are recorded from the dogfood's logs (no titles or paths in the record), with what the viewer saw
Each failure becomes a task in tasks/prd.json, placed before JS-054 when it concerns the segment format
docs/status.md says which clients have played which paths
An HEVC HDR copy and its fallback are played once in a browser with an HEVC decoder (E2E_HEVC=1) and recorded; until then docs/status.md says 'checked with ffmpeg only'
Streamyfin's player entries in compat/clients.yaml are corrected from what the device sends

Fluster, as a released build on at least one desktop platform (the engine named: WebKitGTK, WebView2 or WKWebView), signs in and lists a library against the dogfood or a main-<sha> image, before it plays; recorded with no titles or paths (from JS-144, D-019). A record from Fluster's maintainers through issue #202 counts. A failure becomes a task ahead of every other open task.

On Fluster: a sign-in refused by JS-145 (403 with Retry-After, D-020) reads as 'try again in N minutes', not as a wrong password, a refusal by the administrator or a server fault (from JS-145, D-019); a server address typed with a trailing slash still signs in; whether Fluster asks for the subtitle playlist, and what its viewer sees, is recorded (answers BL-201).

Whether each device's profile declares Dolby Vision is recorded. On one that does: a profile 5 film and a profile 8.1 film from the dogfood are played, with what PlaybackInfo decided (direct play, copy or re-encode) and what the viewer saw. A profile 5 film re-encoded for a client that declares it becomes a task. If neither device declares it, or the dogfood holds no profile 5 film, docs/status.md says profile 5 on a client that declares Dolby Vision is not proven (D-021)
userStories.notes: Needs the owner's devices and about an hour; the lead prepares the test list and reads the logs. Widened by the product owner's direction review (2026-11-19): goals 1 and 3 are claimed for every client and proven for one.

userStories.title: Mixed versions are safe: migrations and spec hashes across a rolling upgrade
userStories.description: Every dogfood deploy already runs two versions side by side, but upgrade safety is one line at the end of the plan (JS-058). Migrations run with no lock timeout and no check for migrations a newer version applied (internal/db/db.go), an old worker can compute another spec hash than a new one (ARCHITECTURE.md known departures), and docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md disagree on which role rolls first.
acceptanceCriteria: Migrations take a lock timeout and a version that finds a migration newer than it knows refuses to start with a clear message
A worker of the previous version and one of this version serve the same stream, in a real-process test, without a spec hash disagreement breaking playback (or the job is refused by the older one)
One documented rollout order, the same in docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md, and a test or check that each migration in a release is safe for the previous version's code

With a stream replica of the previous decision version registered and an api replica of the new one, PlaybackInfo offers nothing the old replica would refuse (a real-process test), and docs/running.md no longer requires an order between api and stream
userStories.notes: Before JS-054, which adds encoder families to the spec. The version-gated claim moved to JS-082 (2026-11-12). Extended from the Fable 5.2 blind audit, 2026-11-14.

userStories.title: File naming against real library layouts: extras, specials and odd names
userStories.description: The naming rules have three tests (internal/library/naming_test.go) and every video in a movies library becomes a Movie (internal/library/scan.go), so extras, featurettes, trailers and samples beside a film are listed as films, and episodes without a season tag are skipped. Metadata files (JS-045) and the Jellyfin import (JS-060) attach to items by path, so the rules must be right first.
acceptanceCriteria: A table of real-world layouts (folders of extras, trailers, samples, specials, multi-episode files, years in names), from Jellyfin's documented naming conventions and observed on a real Jellyfin 12.4, with what each becomes
Extras are not listed as films; specials and season-less episodes are placed as Jellyfin 12.4 places them, or the difference is recorded
No library titles in the fixtures
GET /Items/{itemId}/LocalTrailers lists trailer files stored beside the film, as Jellyfin names them; nothing is fetched from outside the server (#108)

A title that ends in a year-like number keeps it: synthetic table cases 'Harbor Lights 2049 (2017)', 'Harbor.Lights.2049.2017.1080p', 'Harbor Lights 2049' (no year), '2001 Night Garden (1968)', '1888 (2019)' and '2031' give the right title and year, and an existing library's item ids do not change
userStories.notes: Requested by Fluster, the client that ships with jellyscale: #108. Extended from the Fable 5.2 blind audit, 2026-11-14.

userStories.title: Whether a track can be delivered is recorded in Postgres; background extraction per library
userStories.description: Every item detail and PlaybackInfo asks the asset store whether each text track and the fonts manifest exist; subtitles.Exists turns any store error into 'not there', so tracks come and go with store health and the api role needs the asset store only for this. Record deliverability in Postgres when a worker stores a track. Then optional background extraction after a scan, off by default and turned on per library (owner, 2026-11-12), since it costs one full read of every film.
acceptanceCriteria: The api answers which tracks and fonts are listed from Postgres, with no asset-store request, and a store error never hides a track
A library with background extraction on has every text track extracted after a scan, one read per film; one without it extracts on first pick as today
docs/running.md states the setting and its cost
userStories.notes: If it ever copies PGS tracks ahead of time, copying only languages some viewer keeps (JS-118) is the one place hiding would save a film's read. Product owner (2026-11-19): the background extraction stays opt-in, off by default and documented, and uses ranged reads if JS-141 shows they work; the Postgres half does not wait on JS-141.

userStories.title: A stated Postgres connection budget, warned about and measured with many processes
userStories.description: Each worker holds its liveness connection and a hint-listener connection for good plus its pool, so a stock Postgres (max_connections 100) is reached near 45 workers, not the 90 ARCHITECTURE.md states (an estimate from the code, unmeasured). The control-plane ladder ran in one process.
acceptanceCriteria: docs/running.md gives the connection formula per role
A process warns at startup when the cluster's registered processes approach max_connections
A multi-process variant of test/stress.sh measures connections and Postgres load at 50 workers

userStories.title: DOMAINS.md defines the domains; each domain's detail lives with it
userStories.description: DOMAINS.md is 141 KB, with single invariants thousands of words long on one line. Every agent reads it on every task, readers' tools cut its lines short, and it drifts from the code. It becomes the definition of the domains: for each domain its vocabulary, its boundary (what it owns and must not do), and its guarantees as numbered rules of one to three sentences. Each rule's full statement, rationale, measurements, tables, tests and history move whole to one file per domain under docs/domains/, read by tasks that touch that domain. Invariant numbers do not change. Documents and their checks only; no behaviour changes.
acceptanceCriteria: DOMAINS.md is organised by domain: each has its vocabulary, its boundary (owns, must not) and its rules; every invariant belongs to exactly one domain; the preamble says what the file is, that a rule and its section in the domain file bind together, and that a change which bends either updates both in the same change

Every invariant in DOMAINS.md is one to three sentences and at most 600 characters, keeps the number it has today (none renumbered or reused; a new rule takes the next number), and links to its section in its domain file
DOMAINS.md has no line over 600 characters and is under 40 KB in all; no domain file has a line over 1,000 characters
Each domain file under docs/domains/ has one section per rule, headed by the rule's number, holding its full statement, rationale, measurements, tables and the names of its tests
Nothing is lost: a check finds each old invariant's full text under its number in its domain file, and a check lists every old invariant's tests against the new files and fails when one is missing
No guarantee is weakened: a short rule contradicts nothing in its section, and any statement that says less than today's cites a decision id from tasks/decisions.json
Every existing citation still resolves, by a check that fails on a number with no rule: in code, docs/, ARCHITECTURE.md, tasks/prd.json and tasks/decisions.json

The regex-over-prose tests are removed or replaced by tests that compare a constant with the number the doc states; a check that reads a number or table from DOMAINS.md today (the lease table of 25, the window of 37) reads it from where it now lives and still fails when doc and code differ

The pointers change in the same change: CLAUDE.md, the role files in .claude/agents/ (the product owner's read list included) and the build workflow's instructions say every agent reads DOMAINS.md, and a task's agents also read the domain file of each domain the task touches
userStories.notes: Extended from the Fable 5.2 blind audit, 2026-11-14. Amended 2026-11-19 at the owner's request, decided by the product owner (D-017). Starts from a main that holds JS-089's and JS-135/JS-136's DOMAINS edits; a move, not a rewrite; does not hold the people tasks.

userStories.title: A playback id in every log line from PlaybackInfo to each segment
userStories.description: Debugging real-device and failover findings needs to follow one playback through api, stream and worker logs. The first slice of JS-021 and JS-022, moved up.
acceptanceCriteria: PlaybackInfo, the stream requests, the job and the worker's ffmpeg log lines of one playback carry the same id
docs/running.md shows how to follow one playback

userStories.title: One leased job queue for work that is not a segment
userStories.description: Subtitle extraction, fonts, .sup copies and chapter pictures run through subtitle_jobs with lease logic duplicated from transcode jobs and different behaviour (extraction leases are not reaped); internal/transcode holds four subsystems, and encode is about 435 lines. Trickplay and intro detection (JS-052, JS-053) would each add another job kind.
acceptanceCriteria: One media-job table and one claim, lease and reap implementation serve every non-segment job kind
internal/transcode is split into membership, jobs and encode, and encode into named steps
Every existing test of those job kinds passes

encode becomes a job type with named state: no function in internal/transcode is longer than 120 lines (a structure check), and the unreachable branches the audit found (run(begin), next < begin, the stale-file removal) are gone, with the integration and e2e tiers passing with no check changed

Every job kind observes a store failure only where store.Reader gives up (store.InputWithFailure, JS-088): the chapter-picture, subtitle, fonts and .sup jobs no longer wrap the store below the Reader, so a cut the Reader healed never fails a job or skips a chapter (BL-169)
userStories.notes: Extended from the Fable 5.2 blind audit, 2026-11-14.

userStories.title: A nightly full CI run on main
userStories.description: Runner image, browser and mirror drift show up today only in a change's merge-queue run. A scheduled run of the same jobs on main catches them off the merge path, once a day, and supplies timing and flake data.
acceptanceCriteria: A schedule trigger runs every CI job on main once a day, and test/changes.sh treats it as a full run
A failing nightly run opens or updates one issue naming the failed tests

userStories.title: CI's required checks cannot pass by being skipped, and protection has one source
userStories.description: roles has no aggregator, so a skipped roles satisfies the requirement; branch protection lives in both a ruleset and a classic rule that can drift; a pull request touching .github/ or test/**/*.sh is first exercised in the queue; any label restarts a pull request's run.
acceptanceCriteria: roles gets the same decide step as integration and e2e, which fails when its job was skipped for a reason other than a docs-only change
Branch protection is the ruleset alone; the classic rule is removed
A pull request touching .github/ or test/**/*.sh runs the media tiers as ci:full does, and only the ci:full label restarts a run

Its versions match CI's

userStories.title: Recommendations from each viewer's own history, with a reason for each
userStories.description: Fluster, the client that ships with jellyscale, asked (#110) for 'Because you watched...' suggestions. The owner decided (2026-11-12) to build them as the first feature beyond Jellyfin's API: a per-account viewer profile built from watch history on the user's own server, computed by workers and stored in Postgres, with nothing sent outside it, served under the jellyscale namespace (/jellyscale/v1/, PRODUCT.md, #112) that unmodified clients never see. It needs watch history that survives scans (JS-076) and the library's genres, people and similar items (JS-046, JS-049).
acceptanceCriteria: A worker builds and updates each account's viewer profile from that account's watch history only, and nothing leaves the server

GET /jellyscale/v1/recommendations (authenticated as a Jellyfin token) answers suggestions for the signed-in viewer, each with a stated reason ('Because you watched X', a shared genre or person), documented and versioned
No Jellyfin route changes behaviour, and an unmodified Jellyfin client never sees the namespace
A viewer with no history gets a sensible answer (empty or popular in the library), and another account's history never shapes a viewer's suggestions
userStories.notes: First feature under /jellyscale/v1/; Fluster adopts it first.

userStories.title: A settings page for viewers whose app has no place for their track languages
userStories.description: jellyfin-web has no place to turn on hiding tracks outside a viewer's languages, to name the languages to keep, or to show all tracks (JS-118); Fluster has them first. A small page jellyscale serves, linked from jellyfin-web's user menu, gives a browser-only viewer the same switches through the /jellyscale/v1/ settings JS-118 adds.
acceptanceCriteria: A signed-in viewer reaches the page from jellyfin-web's user menu and sees their two opt-ins, their kept languages and 'show all tracks' as saved

Turning an opt-in on with no default language set asks for one first, as Fluster does; the page saves through the same /jellyscale/v1/ route Fluster uses, and the next PlaybackInfo in jellyfin-web reflects it

A viewer whose audio language is saved and whose PlayDefaultAudioTrack is on is told on the page that a film whose default track is in another language still starts in that track (Jellyfin's rule, and its default for every new user), and can turn it off there with one switch, saved through PATCH /jellyscale/v1/users/configuration (JS-123); the next PlaybackInfo in jellyfin-web then names the track in their language
A viewer changes only their own settings; another viewer's are untouched, and an unsigned request is refused
The page works at phone width and in light and dark, with no route outside /jellyscale/v1/ and no change to jellyfin-web's files
userStories.notes: Owner, 2026-11-15: Fluster first, a page later. Planned after the track-language batch so Fluster adopts it first. 2026-11-17 (JS-121's UX review): PlayDefaultAudioTrack defaults to true, so a viewer who only saves a language keeps hearing a film's flagged track, usually its original; the page says so and offers the switch.

userStories.title: A user id in a request names the caller, or the request is refused
userStories.description: About twenty routes take a user id, in the path of the aliases jellyfin-web calls or in a userId query, and ignore it: the answer is the caller's data whatever the id says (routes.go:121, items.go:67). Nothing leaks, but an administrator who asks for another user's list is given their own under the other's name, and no test would notice a handler that started to honour the id without a check. Two handlers that do honour it carry two hand-written copies of the check, in two orders (sessions.go:346-372, user_configuration.go:160-175). This task makes one rule, in one place, before any handler runs.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first: compat/captures/user-scope-12.4.md and .json record, from a real Jellyfin 12.4 with an administrator and two non-administrators, for every route in compat/endpoints.yaml: the status, and whose data came back, when a non-administrator names the other non-administrator (in the path, and as userId in the query), names an id that is no user, names a malformed id, and when the administrator names a non-administrator. It also records what POST /Items/{itemId}/PlaybackInfo does with a UserId in its body and GET /Sessions with controllableByUserId

Route has Users: 'own' (the default) or 'admin-any'. 'admin-any' is exactly GET /Users/{userId}, POST /Users/Configuration, POST /Users/{userId}/Configuration and POST /UserItems/{itemId}/UserData. --print-routes writes user: for every route that is not 'anyone', and docs/access.md's table is held to it

One guard, before the handler: on every 'viewer' route, a user id in the {userId} path segment, the userId query, the controllableByUserId query or PlaybackInfo's body that is not the caller's answers 403 when the route is 'own', whoever asks, administrators included. Nothing is read or written for the other user. The caller's own id, dashed or compact, in any case, answers as with no id

On an 'admin-any' route one helper decides: a non-administrator naming another user gets 403 before any lookup, whether the id is a user or not; an administrator naming a user acts on that user; an administrator naming nobody known gets 404; a malformed id gets 400. sessions.go and user_configuration.go use the helper and hold no copy

TestAccess asks every 'viewer' route with viewer A's token and viewer B's id, in the path where the route has one and as userId in the query on every route: 403 on all of them. With the administrator's token and B's id: 403 on every 'own' route, and B's record on the four 'admin-any' routes. After the whole sweep B's rows in users, user_item_data, display_preferences and sessions are byte for byte what they were
An 'anyone' route ignores a user id: POST /Users/AuthenticateByName?userId={B} signs A in

Named mutants, each failing every run: the guard reads the path and not the query; the guard lets an administrator through on an 'own' route; the helper looks the user up before it refuses a non-administrator

The one case of JS-116's captured replay that changes is named in the pull request: a non-administrator naming an id that is no user on the Configuration routes got 404 as on Jellyfin and now gets 403, so that the answer no longer says whether the id is a user. Every other case passes unchanged
jellyfin-web still works: the e2e tier passes unchanged (it sends its own id everywhere), and the differential tier passes with no new entry, since its one user names itself

DOMAINS.md invariant 49 and the routes.go comment 'These act on the caller whatever userId says' say the new rule. docs/access.md lists, under 'Stricter than Jellyfin', that an administrator is served another user's view on four routes only, with the capture entry that shows Jellyfin serving it everywhere
userStories.notes: Changed answers, to list in the pull request: a request naming another user's id got 200 with the caller's data and now gets 403; the Configuration 404 above. Neither is visible to a viewer using a client, which always sends its own id.Tests make their second user by SQL, as user_configuration_integration_test.go does; no seeding route is added. Jellyfin's rule is RequestHelpers.GetUserId (Jellyfin.Api/Helpers/RequestHelpers.cs:67-81 at v12.4). Owner's decisions (2026-11-16, on Fable 5.2's access model, .results/access-model-fable-2026-11-16.md): pictures by id open to whoever holds the id, by name need a token; per-library access right after JS-033; a revoked or disabled user's running stream stops within 15 s; a viewer sees no other viewer's name; an administrator manages accounts but never browses, plays or reports as another user; a Policy field jellyscale does not enforce is refused when changed (400); 'may download' is honoured; operator keys are never users; no issue is filed on Findroid for now.

userStories.title: A re-encode's x264 preset is part of its spec, and its price follows the preset
userStories.description: Every x264 re-encode uses -preset veryfast (internal/transcode/ffmpeg.go, at both x264 sites). spikes/picture-quality measured faster at +2.5 VMAF on the mean and +3.5 to +5 on the worst frames for 1.2 to 1.6 times the CPU, and medium +0.5 more for 2.2 times. The owner decided (2026-11-19) that operators choose the preset, trading picture against the compute they pay for, with faster the default (JS-136). This task builds what that needs underneath: the spec carries the preset, so every worker that encodes a stream uses the same one (segments of two presets under one init segment fail in Chromium with PIPELINE_ERROR_DECODE, spikes/picture-quality), and Spec.Cost prices each preset from a film measured through a worker, so a worker admits as many jobs as it can keep at real time. The spike also found today's 0.8 cores for a 1080p job low for a hard film (1.36 CPU s per s at veryfast, pinned, unverified basis); this task measures it properly.
acceptanceCriteria: Spec has a preset, one of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; it is part of Spec.Hash, so two specs that differ only in it have different hashes, and a spec stored before the field existed reads as veryfast and keeps its hash, so its stored segments are still served

The preset travels in the playlist and segment URLs as the spec's other fields do, so a request answered by any replica rebuilds the same spec and hash whatever that replica would choose; a test asks one stream's playlist and segments of two api replicas and finds one hash

A worker encodes with the spec's preset, never a setting of its own: a test reads the arguments of a re-encode and of an H.264 copy's fallback (recodeArgs) for two presets and finds each spec's preset in each; the HEVC and AV1 fallbacks keep their own presets and say so in docs/transcoding.md

In a rolling upgrade a worker from before this task never takes a job whose preset is not veryfast (it would encode veryfast under that spec's hash, which Chromium cannot decode after the init segment): a mixed-fleet test with a pinned release-before worker, as JS-030's, gives it a faster job and finds it made by a new worker, while veryfast jobs are still shared by both
A test with real segments: a store holding a stream's segments at one preset never serves them for a spec of another preset; the second spec's job encodes its own

A measurement test, run as the AV1 rows are, logs for each of superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow, from a 1080p and a 4K real-film source, SDR and tone mapped, through a worker's own command, on Ubuntu 24.04's ffmpeg 6.1 and on ffmpeg 9: CPU seconds per second of film, and the time to the first segment and to the fourth on 2 and 4 CPUs; docs/transcoding.md records the figures with the machine and the command

Spec.Cost has a row per preset, SDR and tone mapped, 1080p and 4K, each at or above its measured figure with the margin docs/transcoding.md gives today; the HEVC fallback's x265Extra and the AV1 fallback's rows do not follow the x264 preset; if veryfast's rows are found low and raised, the pull request states, per row, viewers per worker before and after and what the next viewer on a full worker then sees, and the owner approves those numbers before it merges
With real processes: a worker given jobs whose costs add up to its cores, at faster and at medium, keeps each at 1.2 times real time or more without a helper
No viewer-visible change while every spec is veryfast: the transcode, seek and helper e2e scenarios pass as before
userStories.notes: Bump OutputVersion only if the arguments of a veryfast spec change; a spec read from before the field must keep its hash (invariant: stored segments of a spec are its output).

userStories.title: Operators choose the x264 preset, faster by default
userStories.description: The owner (2026-11-19): operators choose the preset, deciding how much picture they give up for the compute they pay for, and faster is the default unless they choose another. JS-135 put the preset in the spec and priced it; this task adds the setting, makes faster the default and shows a viewer gains picture without losing a quick start.
acceptanceCriteria: A config key transcodePreset accepts superfast, veryfast, faster, fast, medium and slow; left out it is faster; any other value stops the start of every role with an error naming the key and the accepted values

PlaybackInfo writes the configured preset into each new spec and its URLs; changing it and restarting gives new playbacks the new preset while a stream already playing keeps its spec's, and two api replicas configured differently each produce streams that play, because every later request carries the preset (JS-135)

docs/running.md gives, for each preset, the measured CPU against veryfast, the time to the first segment (JS-135's measurement) and the picture gain (VMAF from spikes/picture-quality), and says what changing it does to stored segments (new specs, the old swept as any unused spec)

e2e in jellyfin-web, on the same worker: a start and a seek at faster get their first segment no more than 1.8 times later than at veryfast (the spike measured 1.42 to 1.49; medium is about 2.1), each time recorded in the run, and playback does not stall

A picture test on every tier, with ffmpeg's own psnr and ssim filters (CI's ffmpeg 6.1 has no libvmaf): a real-film clip encoded through the worker at faster, against its source under a 4 Mbps cap, has a higher PSNR-Y (the spike measured +0.27 to +0.92 dB) and a higher SSIM than at veryfast
The default change is listed under Changed guarantees: more CPU per viewer (fewer viewers per worker), up to about a second on a start on a full worker, a better picture

userStories.title: An image subtitle copy that a slow store cannot finish within the hour still arrives
userStories.description: D-002 accepted that a film whose image-track copy (JS-089) misses the one-hour limit keeps today's costly seeks into long cues, retried daily, on condition that a task closes the gap. How many films miss the hour, and the dogfood store's read speed, are unmeasured.
acceptanceCriteria: A design is chosen with the product owner, reading JS-143's count, from: a limit that scales with the file's size, a no-progress limit in place of a wall-clock one (a hung store is not a slow one), and a read that resumes where it stopped so retries add up

With a store slow enough that a film's copy needs more than an hour, the copy completes and the film's seeks into long cues then cost what any seek does; a store that hangs still frees its background slot within the no-progress bound
docs/running.md and DOMAINS 51 state the new rule; D-002's remembered failure applies only to what the new rule still cannot finish

userStories.title: Spike: copy a film's image subtitles without reading the whole film
userStories.description: D-003 accepted one whole-film read per film version to copy its image tracks, and the .sup copy reads the film once per track. The scan already keeps the image tracks' cue points (media_sources.image_cues, DOMAINS 51). Can the tracks be copied by ranged reads at those points instead, and for which films?
acceptanceCriteria: For Matroska films with Cues for the subtitle track, and for those without: whether ranged reads at the stored cue points copy every packet of the track, measured against today's whole-film copy (bytes read, time, packets equal)
The same answer for the .sup copy
The same answer for text-track extraction, which today also reads the whole film (it decides what JS-091's background extraction would cost)
A recommendation with what each kind of film would then cost, recorded in spikes/; a follow-up task if it works
userStories.source: decision D-003; product-owner direction review 2026-11-19 (no further whole-film-read trade-off until it reports)

userStories.title: Helm chart, kept in step with the example manifests
userStories.description: The Helm half of the packaging (D-011: both ways, no drift), after JS-056's manifests.
acceptanceCriteria: The Helm chart installs the same on a fresh cluster
The manifests and the chart cannot drift: a test fails when they would deploy different resources (for example, the manifests are the chart rendered with its defaults, checked in)
The chart sizes CNPG's max_connections as JS-056's manifests do, and installing values whose sum exceeds it fails the render

userStories.title: Measure how many films miss the image-subtitle copy's hour, and the store's read speed
userStories.description: A condition of D-002: the gap-closing task (JS-140) must rest on numbers. Measured on the dogfood once JS-089 is deployed.
acceptanceCriteria: Recorded in docs/subtitles.md: the dogfood store's read speed for a large film, and how many of its films with image tracks missed the hour (counts only, no titles)
The figures are cited by JS-140's design choice

userStories.title: The details page's Audio menu lets a viewer pick any audio track they have not hidden
userStories.description: A viewer cannot pick another audio language on a film's details page in jellyfin-web, which Jellyfin 12.4 offers; no decision accepts that loss (product owner triage, 2026-11-19). PRODUCT.md: the audio and subtitles they chose.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first on Jellyfin 12.4: what the details page's Audio menu lists and what picking one does, recorded in compat/captures
The details page's Audio menu lists every audio track the viewer has not hidden, the chosen one selected, as Jellyfin 12.4 does; picking one plays it, in jellyfin-web (e2e)
If an existing invariant stops this for a client reason, the lead brings the product owner a trade-off brief with the cost of keeping the menu before building

userStories.title: No viewer request is answered 500, and no subtitle is refused, across a Postgres switchover
userStories.description: docs/status.md calls Postgres failover done and says requests are held instead of answering 500, but findings say otherwise: a subtitle is refused for 30 s after a read that hit the outage, and a film started from the snapshot ignores the viewer's languages (product owner triage, 2026-11-19).
acceptanceCriteria: During a real Postgres switchover (real processes), no viewer request of a playing film or a starting one is answered 500; each waits or is served as docs/running.md states
A subtitle read that hit the outage is served once Postgres answers, not refused for 30 s
A film started from the snapshot while Postgres is away plays with the viewer's audio and subtitle languages
The cases of BL-062, BL-064, BL-068 and BL-168 each have a check
docs/status.md and docs/running.md say what holds across a switchover, with the check for each

userStories.title: A re-encoded Dolby Vision profile 5 film looks right
userStories.description: The docs disagree about a re-encoded Dolby Vision profile 5 film: DOMAINS 53 and docs/status.md say it is not mapped (green and purple), docs/transcoding.md says it is tone mapped. Nothing was observed. A wrong picture on every client that does not declare Dolby Vision breaks PRODUCT.md's promise that a re-encoded HDR film looks right on an ordinary screen (D-021).
acceptanceCriteria: Observed first on a film truly coded for profile 5: an openly licensed profile 5 sample, or a file the task makes itself and shows to be coded so (its picture decoded without the Dolby Vision data comes out wrong, as DOMAINS 53 describes, and right with it). A film that only carries the label does not count. If neither can be had, the task stops and goes to the product owner; it is never closed on a labelled-only file. Frames are taken through a worker's own re-encode on ffmpeg 6.1 and on ffmpeg 9 and compared with the same frames from a reference that applies the Dolby Vision data; recorded in compat/captures with the measured colour difference, no title or path
A re-encoded profile 5 film's colours are within the stated difference of that reference on every supported ffmpeg, without a GPU on the worker; a check fails when the mapping is removed
If no supported ffmpeg can do it without a GPU, the build stops and a brief goes to the product owner with each option priced, keeping the right picture among them

userStories.title: Measure what a re-encode above 1080 lines costs, and how often a viewer gets a capped one
userStories.description: Every re-encode is H.264 SDR at no more than 1080 lines (DOMAINS 41, for cost). No decision accepted that ceiling, and the cost of keeping a 4K film's height or an HDR film's range in a re-encode is unmeasured: JS-135 measures 4K sources, not 2160-line outputs. A viewer on a 4K or HDR screen whose film must be re-encoded (a burned-in PGS track on a 4K Blu-ray rip included) sees 1080p SDR (D-021).
acceptanceCriteria: Measured through a worker's own command with the 1080 limit lifted for the measurement only, from a 4K real-film source, SDR and HDR, on ffmpeg 6.1 and ffmpeg 9, on 2, 4 and 8 CPUs: H.264 at 1440 and 2160 lines at veryfast and faster, and 10-bit HEVC at 1080 and 2160 lines with the range kept. For each: CPU seconds per second of film, time to the first and the fourth segment, and whether it holds 1.2 times real time alone and with helpers
The HEVC fallback's 1080p and 4K prices are measured on the same real film, and Spec.Cost's rows are raised where found low
Whether jellyfin-web in Chromium plays H.264 at 2160 lines without stalling is observed
What Jellyfin 12.4 sends for the same requests (height, codec, range) is observed and recorded as the baseline, not the target

From the dogfood's logs over at least 14 days, counts only, no titles: re-encodes started; how many had a source above 1080 lines and a client and cap that would have taken more; how many were HDR sources sent to a client that declares HDR; each split by reason (codec, quality cap, burned-in subtitle)
Recorded in docs/transcoding.md with machine and command

The figures go to the product owner as a brief with keeping the source's height and range priced per viewer, on CPU and on a GPU family; its decision names the task that closes the gap or accepts it, and docs/status.md's line is updated
